transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Ramirez (FinEdge Head of ML), Priya Shah (FinEdge Backend Eng), Liam O'Connor (FinEdge SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, we know you got a busy week so we'll try to keep this tight. quick readout from our side on the caching numbers and then dig into tuning.
[00:08] Carlos: yeah thanks Jordan, excited to see where we are, been watching the dashboards.
[00:15] Maya: cool, so quick context — we ran the week-long pilot with the current prompt set you gave us, traffic shaped to your 10k rps burst profile but mainly at 1.2k steady. two key metrics: prefix (or prefix+template) cache hit, and KV cache hit which is for the longer conversation state / retrieval.
[00:30] Priya: just to clarify, prefix cache is the reuse of prompt prefix and model KV entries right?
[00:35] Maya: yeah exactly. sometimes in the tape we call it prefix caching, sometimes prefix-KV; sorry for the naming drift.
[00:45] Maya: so headline numbers — prefix cache hit about ~63% overall, KV cache hit about ~42% on the representative set. latency improvement for cached routes averaged -28% p50 and -18% p95. token cost reduction was around 22% overall when cached.
[01:05] Carlos: 42% KV hit sounds lower than we'd hoped. do we have a breakdown by prompt family?
[01:12] Maya: yes — the hit rate varies a lot by prompt family. the helpdesk / faq group had ~78% prefix hit and ~67% KV hit because those prompts are very templated. whereas the executive summary prompts are more free-form, prefix hit ~31% and KV ~12%.
[01:30] Liam: are we seeing a lot of near-duplicates that the cache misses on because of whitespace or ephemeral metadata?
[01:35] Maya: exactly — a good chunk is prompt surface-level differences: timestamp stamps, user ids, trace ids, slight punctuation differences. we recommend a prompt normalization step — strip transient metadata, canonicalize dates, and use placeholder tokens for IDs. that bumped hit rate ~8-12% in our internal tests.
[01:55] Jordan: also worth noting the KV cache eviction policy — we defaulted to LRU with per-shard TTL 6h. with your workload we saw a slightly higher churn so some hot keys were getting evicted before reuse. bumping TTL to 12h on hot shards increased KV hit by ~5% but memory footprint went up.
[02:20] Priya: memory footprint concerns us — we are on Dedicated pilot but still want to keep within the RAM envelope. what's the cost tradeoff if we increase TTL?
[02:28] Maya: roughly speaking, increasing TTL to 12h increases memory committed by ~18% on our pod profiles. unit cost goes up but tokens saved reduces compute — net depends on your hit delta. we ran a sim in the spreadsheet we shared — look at tab 'ttl-sensitivity'.
[02:45] Carlos: can we do adaptive TTL? only extend for keys with high reuse?
[02:49] Maya: yes — adaptive TTL by frequency is an option. we can mark keys with reuse>n in a moving window and pin them longer. that moves memory only for the actually-reused keys. it adds a little bookkeeping overhead but it's often worth it.
[03:05] Liam: how about shard sizing? we saw some hot-shard hotspots on the graphs.
[03:10] Maya: current shard size was 128MB per shard; increasing number of shards reduces hotspot probability. we can re-shard proactively or use consistent hashing with virtual nodes to spread hotter keys. that's a config change we can apply in the next deploy.
[03:25] Jordan: quick Q on prompt reuse strategy — Carlos, do you have control over canonicalizing prompts upstream? or do you want Redwood to provide a normalization layer?
[03:33] Carlos: team can do some, but our backend engineers prefer a lightweight server-side normalizer rather than changing all producers.
[03:40] Priya: yeah changing producers is painful. a normalization middleware would be easier for us to adopt.
[03:45] Maya: great — we have a 'prompt normalizer' pattern in our docs: strip ephemeral tokens, collapse whitespace, map entity values to placeholders, and optionally hash long contexts to canonical keys. we'll share a sample lambda and a docker sidecar pattern.
[04:00] Jordan: noted — action item for Jordan to share the sample normalizer and updated config.
[04:08] Carlos: thanks, also curious about batching changes — we saw some variance in latency when batching increased.
[04:12] Maya: right — continuous batching helps throughput but can add a few ms to p50. for your latency SLOs (p95 < 350ms) we recommended small max batch sizes for interactive routes and larger for async bulk. also adaptive batching helps based on request arrival curves.
[04:30] Liam: any notes on deterministic outputs and cache staleness?
[04:34] Maya: good point — cached outputs assume deterministic-ish model configs. if you enable sampling or temperature>0.0 then cached tokens might be less useful. we suggested using a 'cacheable' flag per-route: deterministic routes (temperature=0, top_p=0) go into prefix+KV cache; stochastic routes bypass or use separate caching semantics.
[04:55] Priya: we have a mixed profile — about 70% deterministic, 30% stochastic. so caching still helps but we need route-level policies.
[05:05] Jordan: did we talk about the security side? storing KV cache with PII — are we encrypting keys at rest?
[05:12] Maya: yes — for the private pilot we enable KMS-backed encryption at rest and optional HSM for keys. audit logs are enabled and RBAC controls exist for cache read/write ops. Liam: any blockers from SRE?
[05:25] Liam: VPC peering is pending but not blocked; need egress estimates for procurement. I'll take the action to validate egress numbers.
[05:33] Carlos: one more thing — we noticed that some prompts generate long KV state because of long chat histories. any suggestions?
[05:40] Maya: a couple approaches: sliding window truncation, summarization into condensed KV tokens, or checkpointing long conversations to embeddings store + short pointer keys in KV. summarization reduces KV size and often preserves signal for generation.
[05:53] Priya: summarization sounds attractive but we want to be careful about fidelity for legal/regulatory content.
[06:00] Maya: understood — we can scope which conversation types are summarized vs fully retained.
[06:05] Jordan: back to numbers — is there any other quick experiments we should run short-term to increase KV hit?
[06:12] Maya: yes — two low-friction experiments: 1) prompt normalization layer (easy), 2) increase TTL for top 20% hot keys (adaptive). both together in our internal sims pushed KV from 42% to ~58% on similar corpora.
[06:28] Carlos: good. what's effort estimate for Redwood to run the 24h KV stress test?
[06:33] Maya: we've scheduled compute; we just need your canonical prompt set and traffic mix. once we have that we can run and produce logs + summaries in 48 hours.
[06:44] Carlos: we'll push the prompt CSV by Friday.
[06:47] Jordan: perfect. last part — follow-ups and deliverables recap.
[06:52] Jordan: Jordan to share updated caching config + sample normalizer + spreadsheet by Friday 2026-04-09. Maya to run and share 24h KV run results by 2026-04-14. Carlos to provide canonical prompt set by 2026-04-10. Liam to confirm VPC/egress by 2026-04-13.
[07:05] Priya: thumbs up. anything else?
[07:08] Carlos: nope thanks everyone.
[07:10] Jordan: thanks, we'll follow up in email and post the configs to the shared drive. bye.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts observed — 'K V cache' in automatic text, and speaker timestamps approximate. Shared artifacts referenced: 'ttl-sensitivity' tab in spreadsheet (link in chat), sample prompt normalizer (link), perf spreadsheet (link).
